name: Dystopia
scope: Dystopia as the encyclopedias and scholarship on it define it: the political-literary tradition of imagining a society substantially worse than the author's own (dehumanized, fearful, oppressed under totalitarian or authoritarian regimentation, propaganda, surveillance and loss of individuality), written as a warning against a trend or political programme. Britannica traces the modern genre to Zamyatin's We, with Huxley's Brave New World and Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four modelled on it; the Science Fiction Encyclopedia and Encyclopedia.com (Gale) treat it as the negative counterpart of utopia and tie it to anti-utopia, cacotopia and negative utopia; the Dystopia Project takes Lyman Tower Sargent's definition as its starting point. Covers the literary dystopian tradition and the social criticism it carries; excludes post-apocalyptic fiction that has no society to criticise and the loose everyday use of 'dystopia' for any bad situation.

summary: Dystopia is the tradition, mainly literary, of imagining a society much worse than the author's own, marked by oppression, regimentation, loss of individuality and fear, in order to warn readers against a trend or political programme. Britannica traces the modern genre to Zamyatin's We, with Huxley's Brave New World and Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four as its models. The sources describe the genre and what its works fear, not a programme of what society should be, so they settle no statement.
